What changes when we arrive somewhere new with questions instead of answers?", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c092cd5c80cc7ef09d9860", "tabs": [ "69c085d28383a3710d83adf6", "69c092e8c65c13fe74f33726", "69c092f63adef1023cdb365b", "69c0930345fcea86fbc5577d", "69c09310bbd425ed18abf133" ], "main-content": "

I had done this before. Different city, different community — but the same kind of work, and it had gone well. So when I arrived in San Francisco, I came prepared. I had a framework, a track record, and a clear sense of what was needed.

Within six months, I was confused. The approach that had opened doors elsewhere kept finding them closed here.

That confusion, it turned out, was the most important thing that happened to me.

There's a particular kind of confidence that comes from experience. It's not arrogance — it's simply the accumulation of what has worked. You've seen enough to recognize patterns. You know how things tend to go. And in many ways, that experience is genuinely valuable.

But every place carries its own history. Its own wounds. Its own way of seeing. San Francisco is not Portland. The Tenderloin is not the Richmond. The church that flourished in one neighborhood will not automatically flourish in another. And the person who arrives already knowing what a community needs often misses what the community is already doing.

I started over — not with a new program, but with a new posture. I found a local pastor who had served the same six-block radius for twenty years. I stopped presenting and started asking. I learned that the neighborhood had seen outside helpers come and go for decades, each one carrying tools built for somewhere else.

\"The Spirit was already here before you arrived,\" he told me one afternoon. \"Your job is to find out where He's been working, not to start something new.\"

I didn't forget that.

Presence without listening isn't really presence — it's projection. When I enter a neighborhood, a conversation, or a partnership assuming I already understand the landscape, I risk becoming one more voice that speaks before it sees. A contextual orientation begins not with a plan but with a question: What is already here?

This kind of listening isn't passive. It takes discipline to set aside what has worked elsewhere. It requires trusting that the people who live and serve in a place understand it in ways that no amount of outside experience can replicate. I observe. I ask. I collaborate with those who have stayed when others left.

What would it look like to enter your next conversation — with a neighbor, a colleague, a community you're just beginning to know — as a student rather than an expert? Not abandoning what you've learned, but holding it loosely enough to be surprised.

The Spirit is never absent from a place. The question is whether we arrive humble enough to notice.
